title: Chimera
summary: Chimera is a suspected espionage group tracked as G0114 and described in public reporting as active since at least 2018, with targeting that centres on semiconductor manufacturers and airlines in the Asia Pacific region. Reporting assesses the activity as linked to Chinese state interests and as motivated by theft of intellectual property, particularly source code, chip design material and research data, though that attribution rests on victimology and tooling overlap rather than an official public conclusion. The group combines credential theft with custom tooling, uses legitimate remote access and scheduled tasks for persistence, and moves laterally toward servers holding design and code repositories before compressing and removing large volumes of data. It also maintains long dwell times, which means the intrusion is frequently discovered during a review of historical logs rather than in real time. Analysts reconstruct Chimera activity from authentication logs showing service account misuse, endpoint telemetry of credential dumping and archive creation, repository audit trails recording bulk clones and downloads, and outbound transfers whose volume or destination does not match normal business patterns.

beginner.definition: Chimera is the name for a spying group that public reports link to China. It targets companies that make computer chips and airlines in the Asia Pacific region. The name refers to the group, not to a virus or a tool.
beginner.whyItMatters: Chip design files and source code take years to build and cost a lot of money. If a rival copies them, the victim loses its advantage and may never know how it happened. Chimera matters for another reason. This group stays inside a network for a long time and copies data slowly, so a quick scan will not find it. You need to look at the history of who logged in, what they downloaded, and how much data left the building.
howItWorks: The attackers get an initial login, often by stealing credentials or exploiting an exposed service.
They use legitimate remote access tools (software for controlling a computer from elsewhere) to stay connected.
They set up scheduled tasks and services so their access returns after every restart.
They move through the network toward servers that keep design files and source code.
They collect and compress the files into large archives to make copying faster and quieter.
They send the archives to servers they control, often outside normal working hours.
beginner.example: Imagine a library where a reader visits every evening and copies a few pages from a rare book. Nothing is missing from the shelf, so nobody notices. After a year, the reader has a complete copy of a book that took the library decades to assemble. Chimera behaves like that reader. They do not smash the window or empty the shelves. They take the valuable material slowly, page by page, and they look like a normal customer while doing it.
takeaways: Long dwell time means historical logs are often more useful than live alerts.
Watch large archive files and outbound transfers that do not match normal use.
Attribution to a state sponsor is an assessment and should be described with confidence levels.

objectives: Explain what Chimera is and which industries public reporting says it targets.
Describe how credential theft and legitimate remote access combine to give long term access.
Explain why repository audit logs are valuable when investigating intellectual property theft.
Recognise bulk archiving and unusual outbound transfer volume as detection opportunities.
Explain how attribution confidence should be communicated when describing a threat group.
